'''Argonaut Games''' is a British [[video game developer]] founded in 1982. It was known for the [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System|Super NES]] video game ''[[Star Fox (1993 video game)|Star Fox]]'' and its supporting [[Super FX]] chip, and for ''[[Croc: Legend of the Gobbos]]'' and the ''[[Starglider]]'' series. The company was liquidated in late 2004, and ceased to exist in early 2007. It was relaunched in 2024.

==History==
{{quote box | align=right | width=30% | quote=I told them that this is as good as it's going to get unless they let us design some hardware to make the SNES better at 3D. Amazingly, even though I had never done any hardware before, they said YES, and gave me a million bucks to make it happen.|source=—Argonaut founder and Super FX codesigner, Jez San<ref name="Interview with Jez San" />}}
Argonaut Software was founded by teenager [[Jez San]] in September 1982,<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Brookes|first1=Jason|last2=Bielby|first2=Matt|date=May 1993|title=Superplay interview: Jez San, Argonaut|url=https://archive.org/details/Superplay_Issue_07_1993-05_Future_Publishing_GB/page/n25/mode/2up|magazine=[[Super Play]]|location=United Kingdom|publisher=[[Future Publishing]]}}</ref> though his first game, ''Skyline Attack'' for the [[Commodore 64]],<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |url=http://archive.org/details/Sega_Saturn_Magazine_Issue_24_1997-10_EMAP_Images_GB |title=Sega Saturn Magazine |date=October 1997 |pages=60-63 |issue=24}}</ref> was released before the company was officially formed.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=McFerran |first=Damien |date=2019-12-01 |title=Interview: "I Thought Of The Biggest Number I Could Think Of, Which Was A Million Dollars. Then I Doubled It" - Jez San On Argonaut, Nintendo And Star Fox |url=https://www.timeextension.com/features/interview-i-thought-of-the-biggest-number-i-could-think-of-which-was-a-million-dollars-then-i-doubled-it-jez-san-on-argonaut-nintendo-and-sta |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Time Extension |language=en-GB}}</ref> the company name is a play on his name (J. San) and the mythological story of ''[[Jason and the Argonauts (film)|Jason and the Argonauts]]''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Hopkins |first=Nic |date=October 26, 2004 |title=Jez San close to rescue bid for his troubled Argonaut |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/jez-san-close-to-rescue-bid-for-his-troubled-argonaut-dt7fg78kghh |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=The Times |language=en-GB}}</ref> Its head offices were in [[Colindale]], [[London]] and a U.S. branch was located in [[Woodside, California]] in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]].<ref name="Contact1996">{{Cite web |url=http://www.argonaut.com/otherinf/compinfo.html#TopofPage |title=Company Summary |website=Argonaut Games |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19961029064517/http://www.argonaut.com/otherinf/compinfo.html#TopofPage |date=29 October 1996 |access-date=21 May 2016 |archive-date=29 October 1996 |quote=Argonaut Technologies Limited Capitol House, Capitol Way, Colindale, London, NW9 ODZ, United Kingdom" and "Argonaut USA Rich Seidner – Head of US Operations 210 Grandview Drive, Woodside, California, 94062, USA}}</ref>

In 1986, the company released ''[[Starglider]]'' for the [[Atari ST]] and [[Amiga]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eddy |first=Andy |date=May 1987 |title=Starglider |url=https://archive.org/details/1987-05-compute-magazine/page/45/mode/1up |journal=Compute! |volume=9 |issue=84 |pages=46–47 |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> It is widely considered to be the first 3D video game.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=GameSpy: Argonaut Games |url=http://www.gamespy.com/company/025/025343.html |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=www.gamespy.com}}</ref>

In 1990, Argonaut collaborated with Nintendo during the early years of the NES and SNES, a notable incident being when Argonaut submitted a [[proof-of-concept]] method of defeating the [[Game Boy]]'s copyright protection mechanism to Nintendo.<ref name="McFerran">{{cite web|url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2013-07-04-born-slippy-the-making-of-star-fox|title=Born slippy: the making of Star Fox|last=McFerran|first=Damien|date=22 June 2014|work=[[Eurogamer]]|access-date=20 August 2016}}</ref> Argonaut's star programmer Dylan Cuthbert, alongside Nintendo, developed the Japan-only space combat simulation game ''[[X (1992 video game)|X]]'' for the Game Boy in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Andrews |first=Nate |date=September 8, 2011 |title=Influencing the Fox - Feature |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/feature/27708/influencing-the-fox |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref> The game was notable for being one of the few 3D games on the console.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parish |first=Jeremy |date=April 22, 2019 |title=The 25 Greatest Game Boy Games |url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/the-25-greatest-game-boy-games- |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190422223218/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/the-25-greatest-game-boy-games- |archive-date=2019-04-22 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=USgamer.net |language=en}}</ref> An English version called ''Lunar Chase'' was developed but ultimately cancelled.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parrish |first=Jeremy |title=A Bathtub Full of Acid: The Story of How Dylan Cuthbert Went From Making 3D Engines for Game Boy to Star Fox |url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/dylan-cuthbert-star-fox-game-boy-hacking-feature-interview |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024023320/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/dylan-cuthbert-star-fox-game-boy-hacking-feature-interview |archive-date=2022-10-24 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=USgamer.net |language=en}}</ref>

The combined efforts from Argonaut and Nintendo yielded a prototype of the game ''[[Star Fox (1993 video game)|Star Fox]]'', initially codenamed "nesGlider" and inspired by ''Starglider.'' The demo was then ported to the SNES.<ref name="McFerran" /><ref name="Interview with Jez San" /> This ultimately became Star Fox, with [[Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development|Nintendo EAD]] handling design and Argonaut in charge of programming. Three programmers, including Cuthbert, were assigned to work on the game in Japan.<ref name="McFerran" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Machkovech |first=Sam |date=2017-10-03 |title=Original Star Fox staffer tells story of sequel's shelving, surprise launch |url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2017/10/exclusive-legendary-star-fox-coder-on-series-history-surprise-sequel-launch/ |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref>

In order to improve performance from the demo, Nintendo commissioned Argonaut to design custom hardware to give the SNES [[true 3D]] capability. San hired chip designers and made the [[Super FX]] [[Reduced instruction set computer|RISC processor]]. They originally codenamed it the Mathematical Argonaut Rotation I/O, or "MARIO", as is printed on the chip's surface.<ref name="McFerran" /><ref name="Interview with Jez San">{{cite web|last=Bolton|first=Syd|author-link=Syd Bolton|title=Interview with Jez San, OBE|website=Armchair Empire|url=http://www.armchairempire.com/Interviews/jez-san-interview.htm|access-date=16 February 2014|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071217092221/http://www.armchairempire.com/Interviews/jez-san-interview.htm |archive-date=17 December 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Of argonauts, vectors, and flying foxes">{{cite web |url=http://blamethecontrolpad.com/argonaut/argonaut2.htm |title=Of argonauts, vectors, and flying foxes: The rise of 3D on Nintendo consoles |access-date=4 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080613053018/http://blamethecontrolpad.com/argonaut/argonaut2.htm |archive-date=13 June 2008 |url-status=dead |website=Blame the Control Pad}}</ref> The chip was so powerful that Argonaut developers joked the Super NES was just a box to hold the chip.<ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with Jez San |website=Arwing Landing |url=http://www.arwinglanding.net/articles.php?page=writeups/jezsan |access-date=4 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928041355/http://www.arwinglanding.net/articles.php?page=writeups%2Fjezsan |archive-date=28 September 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> 

After building the Super FX, Argonaut designed several different chips for other companies' video game machines, which were never released. These include machines codenamed ''GreenPiece'' and ''CD-I 2'' for [[Philips]], the platform codenamed ''VeggieMagic'' for [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] and [[Toshiba]], and [[Hasbro]]'s "virtual reality" game system codenamed ''MatriArc''.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Plowman |first=Ed |date=2025-09-29 |title=That Time We Nearly Changed Gaming History: Hasbro's VR Project That Almost Was |url=https://medium.com/@edplowman/that-time-we-nearly-changed-gaming-history-hasbros-vr-project-that-almost-was-69a8a6e9e77a |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Medium |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Erl |first=Josef |date=2025-08-05 |title=VR in the 90s: The failed VR goggles from Nintendo, Atari, Sega & Hasbro |url=https://www.heise.de/en/background/VR-in-the-90s-The-failed-VR-goggles-from-Nintendo-Atari-Sega-Hasbro-10510221.html |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=heise online |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Dahad |first=Nitin |date=2020-09-21 |title=ARC: from 3D Game Chips to Licensable RISC Processor |url=https://www.eetimes.com/arc-from-3d-game-chips-to-licensable-risc-processor/ |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=EE Times}}</ref> Additionally, Argonaut built a full-color virtual reality headset for Nintendo, called Super Visor, before the [[Virtual Boy]] was developed.<ref name="McFerran" /> After receiving an investment from [[LSI Logic]], Argonaut was commissioned to design a chip for a potential [[PlayStation 2]] design.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McFerran |first=Damien |date=2019-11-26 |title=The Team Behind Nintendo's Super FX Almost Made the PS2 CPU, And It Was Named After a Dog's Bits |url=https://www.pushsquare.com/news/2019/11/the_team_behind_nintendos_super_fx_almost_made_the_ps2_cpu_and_it_was_named_after_a_dogs_bits |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Push Square |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Argonaut had a three-game deal with Nintendo, leading to the creation of ''[[Stunt Race FX]]''. Cuthbert also worked on ''[[Star Fox 2]]'', which would have introduced more open gameplay and multiple playable characters. The game was mostly completed by 1995, and an updated Super FX chip was designed, but Nintendo ultimately cancelled it due to the emergence of 32-bit consoles.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Klepek |first=Patrick |date=2016-04-18 |title=That Time Nintendo Canceled The Nearly Finished Star Fox 2 |url=https://kotaku.com/that-time-nintendo-canceled-the-nearly-finished-star-fo-1771660162 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=Kotaku |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Dickens |first=Anthony |date=2017-06-26 |title=The Full Story Behind Star Fox 2, Nintendo's Most Famous Cancellation |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2017/06/feature_the_full_story_behind_star_fox_2_nintendos_most_famous_cancellation |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=Nintendo Life |language=en-GB}}</ref> The game was finally released in 2017 on the [[Super NES Classic Edition]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dickens |first=Anthony |date=2017-06-26 |title=Star Fox 2 Will Finally Be Released Thanks To Super NES Classic Edition |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2017/06/star_fox_2_will_finally_be_released_thanks_to_super_nes_classic_edition |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=Nintendo Life |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 1996, John Edelson was hired as the company General Manager. He ran the group for two years, reorganizing the company, cutting costs, and streamlining operations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sillifant |first=Ross |date=2015 |title=John Edelson interview |url=https://www.ataricompendium.com/archives/interviews/john_edelson/interview_john_edelson.html |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=www.ataricompendium.com}}</ref> Capital was raised in 1996–1998 from [[Tom Teichman]] and [[Apax Partners]].<ref name=":4" /> According to Jez San, Argonaut remained an independent developer by choice, and had turned down several buyout offers.<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Rider|first1=David|last2=Semrad|first2=Ed|date=December 1997|title=British Invasion|url=https://retrocdn.net/images/1/15/EGM_US_101.pdf|magazine=[[Electronic Gaming Monthly]]|publisher=[[Ziff Davis]]|issue=101|page=170}}</ref>
[[File:MARIO CHIP 1 Starwing.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Super FX]] chip inside a PAL cartridge of ''[[Star Fox (1993 video game)|Starwing]]'', both developed by Argonaut.]]
In 1997, the company was moved to a new building in Edgware.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.argonaut.com/html/body_argonaut_has_moved_.htm |title=Argonaut Contact information |publisher=Argonaut Games |date=13 January 1998 |access-date=9 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19980113111227/http://www.argonaut.com/html/body_argonaut_has_moved_.htm |archive-date=13 January 1998 |url-status=bot: unknown |quote=Argonaut House 369 Burnt Oak Broadway Edgware Middlesex HA8 5XZ}}</ref> It had about 120 employees at this time. In September 1997, ''[[Croc: Legend of the Gobbos]]'' was released by [[Fox Interactive]] for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] and [[Sega Saturn]]. A PC version of the game was also later released in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Croc |url=http://www.argonaut.com/html/body_croc.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19971211131301/http://www.argonaut.com/html/body_croc.htm |archive-date=1997-12-11 |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=www.argonaut.com}}</ref> The game had previously been pitched to Nintendo as a 3D Yoshi game.<ref name=":7" /><ref name="McFerran" /> 

In 1998, Argonaut Software was split into Argonaut Technologies Limited (ATL) and Argonaut Software Limited (ASL).<ref name=":1" /> With space being a premium at the office on Colindale Avenue, ATL was relocated to an office in the top floor of a separate building. The building was called Capitol House on Capitol Way, just around the corner. There, it continued the design of CPU and GPU products and maintained "[[BRender]]", Argonaut's proprietary software 3D engine.

In 1998, ATL was rebranded ''ARC'' after the name of its main product, the [[ARC (processor)|Argonaut RISC Core]], and became an independent company under founder Rob Clucas and CEO Bob Terwilliger.<ref name=":4" /><!--no, this is not a troll addition, that's his name-->

Argonaut Software Limited became Argonaut Games and was listed on the [[London Stock Exchange]] in 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hong |first=Quang |date=March 1, 2000 |title=Argonaut Goes Public |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/argonaut-goes-public |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=Game Developer |language=en}}</ref> Intended to be a tie-in game for the [[Alien Resurrection|1997 movie]], ''[[Alien Resurrection (video game)|Alien Resurrection]]'' spent four years in development before it was released in 2000. The game had been a top-down shooter and third-person shooter before ultimately being released as a first-person shooter.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Reilly |first=Luke |date=2024-08-15 |title=The Terrifying (and Sometimes Terrible) History of Alien Games |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/the-terrifying-and-sometimes-terrible-history-of-alien-games |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref> In 2000, the company purchased the recently-founded Just Add Monsters.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Andrew |date=November 14, 2004 |title=Just Add Monsters Morphs Into Ninja Theory |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/just-add-monsters-morphs-into-ninja-theory |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Game Developer |language=en}}</ref> It also acquired the UK-based LTStudios in 2001 to work on PlayStation 2 games.<ref name=":8" />

In 2001, Argonaut developed ''[[Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (PlayStation video game)|Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone]]'' for Electronic Arts.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Herold |first=Charles |date=2001-12-13 |title=GAME THEORY; The Owls You Know, the Devil You Don't |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/12/13/technology/game-theory-the-owls-you-know-the-devil-you-don-t.html |access-date=2026-07-19 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The game was well received and went on to sell eight million units by 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 21, 2003 |title=Ownt.com - Game Stats |url=http://www.ownt.com/qtakes/2003/gamestats/gamestats.shtm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060221044930/http://www.ownt.com/qtakes/2003/gamestats/gamestats.shtm |archive-date=2006-02-21 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=www.ownt.com}}</ref> It purchased [[Particle Systems]], a two-person development team in Sheffield, in January 2002.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Gibson |first=Nick |date=May 4, 2000 |title=Argonaut News 2000/1 |url=http://www.gamesinvestor.com/Companies/Past_Coverage/Argonaut/Argonaut_News_2000_1/argonaut_news_2000_1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050316073407/http://www.gamesinvestor.com/Companies/Past_Coverage/Argonaut/Argonaut_News_2000_1/argonaut_news_2000_1.html |archive-date=2005-03-16 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=www.gamesinvestor.com}}</ref>

The company's last game proved to be [[Malice (2004 video game)|''Malice'']] for PlayStation 2 and Xbox. It was originally expected to be released in 2002 by [[Vivendi Games|Vivendi]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=IGN |date=2002-06-07 |title=Malice E3 Impressions |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/06/07/malice-e3-impressions |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref> but spent six years in development.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Caoili |first=Eric |date=March 5, 2010 |title=Curioser And Curioser: Malice's Unreleased PS1 Edition |url=http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2010/03/curioser_and_curioser_malices.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112094550/http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2010/03/curioser_and_curioser_malices.php |archive-date=2020-01-12 |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=GameSetWatch}}</ref> It was cancelled by Argonaut in 2003. At the same time, the cancellation and delay of several other projects put the company in financial distress.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=I. G. N. |date=2003-05-30 |title=Argonaut Officially Cans Malice |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/05/30/argonaut-officially-cans-malice |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref> ''Malice'' was later picked up by [[ZeniMax Media]] in 2004 and quietly released that June.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=I. G. N. |date=2004-01-23 |title=Remember Malice? |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/01/23/remember-malice |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=David |date=2004-06-02 |title=Malice Slips to Retail |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/06/02/malice-slips-to-retail |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref>

In October 2004, Argonaut Games halted trading on the London Stock Exchange.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Feldman |first=Curt |date=October 15, 2004 |title=Argonaut trading halted on London Exchange |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/argonaut-trading-halted-on-london-exchange/1100-6110667/ |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=GameSpot |language=en-US}}</ref> It called in receivers David Rubin & Partners, placed its subsidiaries Argonaut Software into administration, and put them up for sale. The studio in Sheffield was closed. San resigned from the board of directors<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Andrew |date=October 24, 2004 |title=Argonaut Officially Announces Move Into Administration |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/argonaut-officially-announces-move-into-administration |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=Game Developer |language=en}}</ref> and purchased subsidiaries Just Add Monsters and Morpheme.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fahey |first=Rob |date=2004-10-29 |title=San acquires Morpheme and Just Add Monsters |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/san-acquires-morpheme-and-just-add-monsters |access-date=2026-07-18 |website=GamesIndustry.biz |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> With no buyer for Argonaut Software, all remaining employees were laid off.<ref>{{cite web|last=Jenkins|first=David|date=3 November 2004|title=Remaining Argonaut Development Staff Laid Off|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/remaining-argonaut-development-staff-laid-off|access-date=1 February 2018|website=[[Gamasutra]]}}</ref> Just Add Monsters became Ninja Theory in November.<ref name=":3" /> 

Studio leaders went on to form [[Rocksteady Studios]] and many former employees would join the developer.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fahey |first=Rob |date=2005-01-17 |title=Roll Call back on track as SCi funds new development studio |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/roll-call-back-on-track-as-sci-funds-new-development-studio |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=GamesIndustry.biz |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Burnes |first=Andrew |date=2005-01-17 |title=SCi Invests In Ex-Argonaut Start-Up |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2005/01/17/sci-invests-in-ex-argonaut-start-up |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref> Argonaut was officially  dissolved in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Scullion |first=Chris |date=2025-07-01 |title=Croc studio Argonaut wants to remaster cult N64 shooter Buck Bumble |url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/croc-studio-argonaut-wants-to-remaster-cult-n64-shooter-buck-bumble/ |access-date=2026-07-21 |website=VGC |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Reopening (2024–present)===
On 28 August 2024, Jez San reopened Argonaut Games as a boutique publisher that would focus on re-releasing and remastering Argonaut's existing franchises alongside the publication of third-party independent titles. Its first release is a remaster of ''Croc: Legend of the Gobbos'',<ref name="CrocRemaster">{{Cite web |last=Romano |first=Sal |date=2024-08-28 |title=Croc: Legend of the Gobbos remaster announced for consoles, PC alongside Argonaut Games revival |url=https://www.gematsu.com/2024/08/croc-legend-of-the-gobbos-remaster-announced-for-consoles-pc-alongside-argonaut-games-revival |access-date=2024-08-28 |website=Gematsu |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=McEvoy |first=Sophie |date=2024-08-29 |title=Argonaut Games returns as publisher after 20 year hiatus |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/argonaut-games-returns-as-publisher-after-20-year-hiatus |access-date=2026-07-19 |website=GamesIndustry.biz |language=en}}</ref> which had previously been teased by San the previous year.<ref>{{cite web |last1=McFerran |first1=Damien |title=Croc HD Is In Development, Says Argonaut Founder Jez San |url=https://www.timeextension.com/news/2023/06/croc-hd-is-in-development-says-argonaut-founder-jez-san |website=Time Extension |publisher=[[Hookshot Media]] |access-date=7 June 2023 |date=7 June 2023 |archive-date=7 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230607090145/https://www.timeextension.com/news/2023/06/croc-hd-is-in-development-says-argonaut-founder-jez-san |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite tweet<!--This is the primary source relied on by McFerran above--> |user=aerobatic |number=1666119518949715969|title=I have news but it's a little premature to announce it. a 'Croc HD' has started early development. |language=en |url=https://twitter.com/aerobatic/status/1666119518949715969 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230607161815/https://twitter.com/aerobatic/status/1666119518949715969 |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 7, 2023 |date=June 6, 2023}}</ref>

On 25 September 2024, Argonaut announced it had made a strategic investment in Ancient Machine, the developer of the forthcoming PC narco-thriller ''VICE Undercover''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-09-25 |title=Argonaut Games (@ArgonautGames_) on X |url=https://x.com/ArgonautGames_/status/1838988037390221542 |access-date=2026-07-18 |work=X (formerly Twitter) |language=en-US |quote=Argonaut Games has teamed up with Indie Developer Ancient Machine to help launch its forthcoming debut game, @VICE_Undercover, a deep narrative-driven narco thriller that aims to redefine the point-and-click adventure genre.}}</ref>

==BRender==
[[File:Microsoft 3D Movie Maker 640x480.jpg|thumb|[[3D Movie Maker]], developed by [[Microsoft]], runs on BRender.]]
BRender (abbreviation of "Blazing Renderer") is a development toolkit and a realtime 3D [[Game engine|graphics engine]] for computer games, simulators, and graphic tools. It was developed and licensed by Argonaut Software.<ref>{{cite web|title=BRender Web page|publisher=Argonaut Software|url=http://www.argonaut.com/brender/index.html|access-date=22 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19961029050559/http://www.argonaut.com/brender/index.html|archive-date=29 October 1996}}</ref> The engine supports [[Intel]]'s [[MMX (instruction set)|MMX]] instruction set and [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]], [[MS-DOS]], and [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] platforms. Support for 3D hardware [[graphics accelerator card]]s was added.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Wave Report on Digital Media Issue 606 8/16/96|publisher=4th WAVE, Inc.|url=http://www.3dlinks.com/waveissue.cfm?issue=606#voodoo|access-date=22 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707063518/http://www.3dlinks.com/waveissue.cfm?issue=606#voodoo|archive-date=7 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> Software made with BRender includes ''[[Carmageddon]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine|date=January 1997|title=NG Alphas: Carmaggedon|url=https://archive.org/details/NEXT_Generation_25/page/n125/mode/2up|magazine=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]|issue=25|pages=125–6}}</ref> ''[[Croc: Legend of the Gobbos]]'', ''[[FX Fighter]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine|date=May 1995|title=3D Graphics Help|url=https://archive.org/details/GamePro_Issue_070_May_1995/page/n139/mode/2up|magazine=[[GamePro]]|publisher=[[International Data Group|IDG]]|issue=80|page=139}}</ref> ''[[I-War (1997 video game)|I-War]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine|date=October 1997|title=NG Alphas: I-War|url=https://archive.org/details/NEXT_Generation_34/page/n107/mode/2up|magazine=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]|issue=34|page=104}}</ref> and ''[[3D Movie Maker]]''. It was released as [[free and open-source software]] under the [[MIT License]] on 3 May 2022.<ref>{{Cite tweet |last=Averlong |first=Alice |user=Foone |number=1521574394761383936 |date=2022-05-03 |title=I just got approval from Jez San, former CEO of Argonaut Games, to open source the BRender engine. |access-date=2022-05-04 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220504050032/https://twitter.com/Foone/status/1521574394761383936 |archive-date=2022-05-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wright |first=Steven |date=2022-05-04 |title=At last, Microsoft 3D Movie Maker is now open-source... Wait, what? |url=https://www.inputmag.com/gaming/microsoft-3d-movie-maker-croc-carmageddon-open-source |access-date=2022-05-05 |website=Input |language=en}}</ref>

extract: Argonaut Games is a British video game developer founded in 1982. It was known for the Super NES video game Star Fox and its supporting Super FX chip, and for Croc: Legend of the Gobbos and the Starglider series. The company was liquidated in late 2004, and ceased to exist in early 2007. It was relaunched in 2024.
